summary: “Is Earth okay?” is an interactive dashboard that turns NASA and NOAA observations into a plain answer for any place on the planet. You pick a measurement on the left: air temperature, rainfall, soil moisture, sea ice, sea level, ocean heat, ocean acidity, currents and 30 more. Then you pick a place on a 3D globe, from a single spot to a country, a sea or a hand-drawn area. The dashboard answers on the right in the words of its name: “Not really okay: +0.4 °C per decade” or “Looks fine here”. Next to the answer it shows a chart of every year with its trend line.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

"Is Earth okay?" is an interactive dashboard that turns NASA and NOAA observations into a plain answer for any place on the planet. You pick a measurement on the left and a place on a 3D globe: a point, a city, a country, a sea or a hand-drawn area. The right side answers how fast it is changing, whether the change is real or just year-to-year noise, and shows a chart of every year with its trend line.


HOW WE BUILT IT

1. Picked the measurements. We chose 36 variables from NASA missions and models (MERRA-2, GLDAS, GPM IMERG, MODIS, GRACE) and from NOAA and partner ocean products (OISST, NSIDC sea ice, EN4 ocean heat, OceanSODA pH). Each one comes with a short plain-language definition.

2. Built one common dataset. Ingest scripts download every source and regrid it to the same 1° monthly grid for 2000–2025. They compute annual means and precompute trend maps. Everything is published as an open dataset on Hugging Face, so anyone can reproduce our numbers.

3. Chose statistics a scientist would accept:
- Mann-Kendall test with Sen's slope, corrected for autocorrelation;
- false-discovery-rate control, because thousands of grid cells are tested at once;
- area-weighted averages for countries, seas and hand-drawn boxes;
- quick-analysis checks: is it a steady trend or one jump, does it hold from any start year.

4. Built the API. It runs on FastAPI and reads the dataset straight from the Hub with ranged reads.

5. Built the dashboard. It is React with a WebGL globe: pick a measurement on the left, pick a place on the globe, and read the answer, the chart and the checks on the right. A game-style tutorial guides first-time users, and the app warns about illogical picks, such as ocean data on a city.

6. Validated the results. We compared grid trends with over 1,000 NOAA weather stations, and checked that the dashboard reproduces published findings: global burned area falling, China and India greening, and Antarctic sea ice dropping in 2016.


BENEFITS AND WHO IT IS FOR

- Students and teachers work with real NASA data, with statistical significance explained in plain words.
- Journalists can check a claim like "this region is drying out" in seconds, with the uncertainty shown.
- Anyone curious gets an honest answer to "Is Earth okay?" for their own place.


INTENDED IMPACT

Climate data is public but hard to read, so most people rely on headlines. We want anyone to be able to check a climate claim about their own place in under a minute.


TOOLS WE USED

- Languages: Python and TypeScript.
- Backend and data: FastAPI, Pandas, NumPy, SciPy, pyMannKendall, PyArrow, Hugging Face Hub.
- Frontend: React, Vite, Three.js / React Three Fiber, ECharts, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Zustand.
- Hosting: Vercel (web), Render (API), GitHub (code), Hugging Face (dataset).
- AI assistant: Claude Code.
- Hardware: our own laptops; no special hardware.


WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

The app answers a human question, "Is Earth okay?", instead of showing a raw chart. The statistics are shown as a detective's checklist: is it a steady trend or one sudden jump, does it survive a different start year, does a second dataset agree. A game-style tutorial teaches the three moves in 30 seconds. And the same globe shows how one process can push a variable up in one place and down in another, which is exactly what the challenge asks people to discover.


FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Honest answers: we only call a change real when the data clearly shows it, not when it could be ordinary ups and downs. The app also warns when a change looks like a sudden jump caused by a new satellite or a model update rather than by the climate.
- Thousands of places at once: when you check that many places, some will look like they are changing just by chance. We correct for that, so the map does not light up with fake trends.
- One consistent dataset: every measurement uses the same grid and the same years, and the data is fixed to one version, so everyone sees the same numbers.
- The audience: simple definitions, a guided tutorial, and clear messages when a pick makes no sense, such as ocean data on a city.
- Speed on a free server: the heavy calculations are done in advance, so the app answers quickly even on free hosting.


WHAT'S NEXT

- Forecasting: extend each trend a few years ahead with machine-learning and statistical models, always with an uncertainty band, and compare the result with official climate projections (CMIP6) for the same place.
- Explaining the cause: link changes between variables, for example rain versus heat for soil moisture, to suggest what drives a trend.
- More data and detail: air pollution (NO2), night lights and finer resolution for cities.
- More languages, starting with Ukrainian, and classroom-ready lessons for teachers.
